exercises.prompt: Implement unique(arr) so it returns a Set of arr's distinct values, with duplicates collapsed. unique([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]) is a Set containing 1, 2, and 3. An empty array returns an empty Set.
hints: A Set stores each value at most once, so it dedupes for free — the question is how to get your array's values into one.
The Set constructor takes any iterable and keeps only distinct values: new Set([1, 1, 2]) already holds just 1 and 2.
return new Set(arr) — returning a plain array instead would fail, because a Set is compared by size and membership, not by order.

exercises.prompt: Implement union(a, b), where a and b are arrays, so it returns a Set of every value that appears in either array, with duplicates collapsed. union([1, 2], [2, 3]) is a Set containing 1, 2, and 3. Two empty arrays return an empty Set.
hints: If you had a single array holding everything from both a and b, a Set would remove the overlap automatically.
Spread both arrays into one: [...a, ...b] concatenates them, then hand that to the Set constructor.
return new Set([...a, ...b]) — the size test proves the value shared by both arrays is counted only once.

exercises.prompt: Implement intersection(a, b), where a and b are arrays, so it returns a Set of the values that appear in BOTH arrays, with duplicates collapsed. intersection([1, 2, 3], [2, 3, 4]) is a Set containing 2 and 3. If the arrays share nothing, or either is empty, the result is an empty Set.
hints: To keep a value from a, you need a fast way to ask 'is this also in b?' — a Set of b answers that in one call.
Turn b into a Set, then filter a down to the values that Set contains: a.filter(x => setB.has(x)).
const setB = new Set(b); return new Set(a.filter(x => setB.has(x))) — wrapping the filtered result in a Set collapses any duplicates that a carried.

exercises.prompt: Implement difference(a, b), where a and b are arrays, so it returns a Set of the values that appear in a but NOT in b, with duplicates collapsed. difference([1, 2, 3], [2]) is a Set containing 1 and 3. If every value of a is also in b, or a is empty, the result is an empty Set.
hints: This is the intersection move with the test flipped: keep the values of a that are NOT in b.
Make a Set of b for quick lookups, then filter a with the negated check: a.filter(x => !setB.has(x)).
const setB = new Set(b); return new Set(a.filter(x => !setB.has(x))) — the membership test confirms a value present in b is absent from the result.

exercises.prompt: Implement wordCounts(words), where words is an array of strings, so it returns a Map from each word to how many times it appears. wordCounts(['a', 'b', 'a']) is a Map with 'a' → 2 and 'b' → 1. An empty array returns an empty Map. Return a Map, not a plain object.
hints: A Map reads and writes keyed values with .get(key) and .set(key, value), the same tally idea as an object but with method calls.
For each word, set its count to the previous count plus one: counts.set(w, (counts.get(w) || 0) + 1), where || 0 covers the first sighting.
Build a new Map(), loop the words updating counts.set(w, (counts.get(w) || 0) + 1), then return counts — a plain object would fail, since the tests check .get and .size.

exercises.prompt: Implement firstDuplicate(arr) so it returns the first value that has already been seen earlier in arr — that is, the value whose second occurrence comes soonest. firstDuplicate([1, 2, 3, 2, 1]) is 2, because 2 repeats before 1 does. If every value is distinct, or arr is empty, return null. Track what you have seen with a Set.
hints: Walk the array once, remembering every value you have passed so you can recognize a repeat the instant it arrives.
A Set is the memory: before recording the current value, check whether it is already there — if so, that is your answer.
for (const x of arr) { if (seen.has(x)) return x; seen.add(x) }  then return null — returning inside the loop catches the earliest second occurrence, not the first-appearing value.
